planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall; prune immediately after the main spring flush to shape and encourage rebloom.

directions: Carnaval is unusual among weigelas for opening flowers in three colors at once, with white, pink, and deep red blossoms appearing together on the same branch in late spring. The mixed-color effect comes from individual flowers aging from pale to dark as they mature, giving the shrub a speckled, festive look rather than a single uniform hue. A rounded, dense habit and scattered light rebloom in summer make it useful as a specimen or informal hedge. Prune immediately after the main spring bloom to shape the plant and encourage the sparse secondary flush.

common_name: French Lace Weigela (Gold-Margined Variegated Weigela with Deep Red Flowers)

planting.note: Site in full sun for strongest leaf variegation and heaviest bloom; tolerates clay if drainage is adequate.

directions: French Lace carries lime-green leaves rimmed in bright gold with a thin red picotee edge, giving the foliage a lacy, two-toned look all season. Clusters of trumpet-shaped, dark red flowers that fade to deep pink in the throat cover the branches in late spring, contrasting sharply with the variegated leaves. Foliage often picks up orange and red tones as autumn approaches, extending the shrub's seasonal interest beyond bloom time. Full sun keeps both the variegation and the flower color at their most vivid.

planting.note: Give ample room for its spreading habit; prune after bloom to control size and renew flowering wood.

directions: Pink Princess produces an abundance of funnel-shaped, lavender-pink flowers with a paler throat along arching branches in late spring and early summer. Its plain dark green foliage and spreading, informal habit make it a reliable background shrub rather than a specialty accent plant. Established plants tolerate a wide range of soils and need little more than occasional post-bloom pruning to stay full and floriferous. It is also the parent of several variegated sports, including Sunny Princess.

common_name: Sunny Princess Weigela (Gold-Margined Variegated Sport of Pink Princess)

planting.note: Full sun brings out the strongest gold leaf margin and heaviest bloom on this compact form.

directions: Sunny Princess is a variegated sport of Pink Princess, carrying the same rose-pink spring flowers but paired with foliage edged in a thin band of bright gold. The narrow gold margin brightens the compact, rounded mound of green leaves through the growing season, well after the main flower flush has passed. Its smaller stature compared to the straight species makes it a good fit for foundation plantings or smaller borders. Full sun brings out the strongest leaf variegation and the heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Allow generous room for its large spreading mature size; renewal-prune older stems every few years.

directions: Candida is a large, spreading selection valued for pure white, funnel-shaped flowers that stand out against bright green foliage in late spring. Unlike the many pink- and red-flowered weigela cultivars, its clean white blooms give it a cooler, more restrained look suited to white or moon gardens. The shrub reaches a substantial size at maturity, so it needs more room than compact modern cultivars and benefits from renewal pruning every few years to keep the center open. It flowers most heavily in full sun on well-drained soil.

planting.note: Prune immediately after flowering since bloom forms on the previous year's wood; allow room for its large mature spread.

directions: Gold Charm opens in earliest spring with a dense covering of golden-yellow, bell-shaped flowers whose throats are flushed with orange, giving the display extra depth compared to plainer yellow forsythias. Flowers appear on bare branches well before the leaves emerge, then the plant fills out into a vigorous, upright-spreading mound of green summer foliage. Its large mature size makes it well suited to informal hedges, screens, or naturalized borders rather than tight foundation plantings. Prune right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Shape immediately after flowering, since bloom forms on old wood; the cutleaf foliage is the main season-long feature.

directions: Tremonia is grown primarily for its deeply incised, almost fern-like dark green leaves, a distinctive cutleaf form rarely seen in other forsythia cultivars. In late winter to early spring it still produces a full crop of bright, lemon-yellow flowers on bare stems before the unusual foliage emerges. The densely branched, upright habit holds its shape well through the season, and the cut leaves continue to set it apart from typical border forsythias all summer. Like other forsythias, it blooms on old wood, so any shaping should happen immediately after flowering.
